about: Single source for every term we use. scripts/docs.py builds docs/reference/0004-glossary.md from this file, and the dashboard's Learn tab reads it directly. Each term has three views: simple (explain it to a ten year old), analogy (something from everyday life), and precise (what an economist or statistician would write).

terms.simple: How much of one country's money you get for another country's money. If 1 euro buys 1.12 US dollars, that is the exchange rate.
terms.analogy: Like swapping trading cards with a friend. Some days your card is worth two of theirs, some days only one, depending on how much people want each card.
terms.precise: The price of one currency in units of another. We store every rate as US dollars per one unit of the foreign currency, so a rising number means the foreign currency got stronger.

terms.simple: Two currencies traded against each other, like euros and dollars. Buying one always means selling the other.
terms.analogy: A seesaw. If one side goes up, the other side goes down.
terms.precise: A quote such as EUR/USD gives the price of the first (base) currency in the second (quote) currency. A long EUR/USD position gains when the euro rises against the dollar.

terms.simple: The ten most traded currencies in the world: US dollar, euro, Japanese yen, British pound, Swiss franc, Canadian dollar, Australian dollar, New Zealand dollar, Norwegian krone and Swedish krona.
terms.analogy: The big, busy shops on the main street. Lots of people trade there, so prices are fair and it is cheap to buy and sell.
terms.precise: The group of developed-market currencies with the deepest markets and tightest spreads. We use the nine non-dollar G10 currencies against the US dollar.

terms.simple: The exchange rate for swapping money right now.
terms.analogy: The price on the sticker today, as opposed to a price agreed for next month.
terms.precise: The rate for immediate delivery, which in FX means settlement two business days later.

terms.simple: An exchange rate agreed today for a swap that happens later.
terms.analogy: Booking a holiday now at a fixed price, even though you travel in three months.
terms.precise: The rate for delivery at a future date. By covered interest parity it equals the spot rate adjusted by the interest rate gap between the two currencies over that period.

terms.simple: What a bank pays you for keeping your money there, or what you pay to borrow. Every country's currency has its own interest rate.
terms.analogy: Rent for money. If you lend your money out, you get rent. If you borrow, you pay rent.
terms.precise: We use the 3-month interbank rate from the OECD for each currency: the rate banks charge each other to borrow for three months. It tracks the central bank's policy rate closely.

terms.simple: The bank in charge of a country's money. It sets the main interest rate, like the Federal Reserve in the US.
terms.analogy: The referee who decides how expensive it is to borrow money in that country.
terms.precise: The institution that sets monetary policy, mainly through a short-term policy rate. Its decisions move interest rates and therefore exchange rates.

terms.simple: The group at the US central bank that meets eight times a year to decide US interest rates.
terms.analogy: A scheduled family meeting where the house rules for the next few months get decided. Everyone waits to hear the result.
terms.precise: The Federal Open Market Committee. Its scheduled announcements are among the biggest regular events for the dollar. See HYP-0006.

terms.simple: The interest you earn on the currency you hold minus the interest you pay on the one you borrowed to buy it.
terms.analogy: Borrowing money from a friend who charges you 1% and putting it in a bank that pays you 5%. The 4% gap is the carry, as long as nothing else changes.
terms.precise: The return a position earns if prices do not move. For a long foreign currency position funded in dollars, carry is roughly the foreign interest rate minus the US rate. Our backtester credits it daily.

terms.simple: Borrowing in a currency with a low interest rate and putting the money in a currency with a high interest rate, to pocket the difference.
terms.analogy: Picking up coins in front of a steamroller. You collect a little almost every day, and once in a while you get flattened.
terms.precise: A long position in high-yield currencies funded by short positions in low-yield ones. It has paid on average but with large losses in risk-off episodes (Brunnermeier, Nagel and Pedersen, 2008). Tested in HYP-0001.

terms.simple: A rule that says you cannot make free money by borrowing in one currency and lending in another if you lock in the future exchange rate today.
terms.analogy: If two shops sell the same toy, and one shop also lets you return it later at a fixed price, the prices have to line up or everyone would game it.
terms.precise: The forward premium equals the interest rate differential, otherwise there is a riskless arbitrage. It holds closely in normal times, with small, persistent deviations since 2008.

terms.simple: A theory that says a currency with a high interest rate should lose value by about as much as the extra interest, so on average you cannot win by chasing high rates. In real data, this mostly does not happen.
terms.analogy: A theory that the shop with the bigger discount will always run out of stock, so the discount never really helps you. In practice the discount often does help.
terms.precise: The expected change in the spot rate equals the interest differential. Empirically the coefficient is close to zero or negative (Fama, 1984), which is the forward premium puzzle and the reason carry trades have paid.

terms.simple: The idea that the same basket of things should cost about the same everywhere once you convert the money. If a burger is much cheaper in one country, its currency is probably too cheap.
terms.analogy: If lemonade costs 1 dollar on your street and 3 dollars on the next one, people would walk over and the prices would move closer.
terms.precise: Exchange rates converge toward the level that equalises price levels. Deviations are large and halve only every three to five years, so PPP is a weak short-run signal but a basis for currency value strategies.

terms.simple: The exchange rate after accounting for how expensive things are in each country.
terms.analogy: Not just how many coins you get, but how much candy those coins actually buy.
terms.precise: The nominal rate multiplied by the ratio of price levels. It is the measure PPP says should be stable over the long run.

terms.simple: How much a country gets for what it sells to other countries compared with what it pays for what it buys from them.
terms.analogy: If you sell lemonade and buy lemons, your terms of trade improve when lemonade prices go up or lemon prices go down.
terms.precise: The ratio of export prices to import prices. A rise tends to strengthen the currency, which is the economic basis for HYP-0003.

terms.simple: A raw material that is the same no matter who sells it, like oil, natural gas, copper, wheat or gold.
terms.analogy: A barrel of oil is like a plain pencil: one is as good as another, so they all sell for the same price.
terms.precise: A standardised, interchangeable good traded on spot and futures markets. We use WTI and Brent crude, Henry Hub gas and copper prices from FRED.

terms.simple: The two most common prices for crude oil. WTI is oil from the United States, Brent is oil from the North Sea near Norway and the UK.
terms.analogy: Two well-known brands of the same thing. They usually cost about the same and move together.
terms.precise: Benchmark crude grades. WTI (West Texas Intermediate) is priced at Cushing, Oklahoma; Brent is the global seaborne benchmark. WTI settled below zero on 2020-04-20 when storage ran out.

terms.simple: The main price for natural gas in the United States.
terms.analogy: The gas price everyone in the US checks, like the price on the big sign at the busiest petrol station.
terms.precise: The delivery point in Louisiana whose spot price is the benchmark for US natural gas. Not the European price, which matters more for Norway.

terms.simple: Money from a country that sells a lot of one raw material, so the currency goes up and down with that material's price. Canada and Norway with oil, Australia with metals, New Zealand with dairy.
terms.analogy: A lemonade stand's pocket money goes up in summer when lemonade sells well. The country's money is the pocket money, and the commodity is the lemonade.
terms.precise: A currency whose value is strongly linked to world prices of the issuing country's main exports (Chen and Rogoff, 2003). The link is strongest at short horizons and has changed since 2020 (Rees, 2025).

terms.simple: A list of about 500 of the biggest companies in the US. Its value is the usual way to say how the US stock market is doing.
terms.analogy: A giant basket with a slice of 500 big companies in it. If most of them do well, the basket gets heavier.
terms.precise: A market-capitalisation weighted US equity index. We use SPY, an ETF that tracks it, with dividends reinvested, as our benchmark.

terms.simple: A fund you can buy like a single share, which holds lots of things inside it. SPY holds all the S&P 500 companies.
terms.analogy: A lunchbox with a bit of everything. You buy the box instead of each item one by one.
terms.precise: An exchange-traded fund. SPY is the oldest and largest S&P 500 ETF, trading since 1993.
terms.risk: An ETF is only as good as what it holds and what it charges. Narrow, new or leveraged ETFs can behave very differently from a broad index fund.

terms.simple: Counting both the price going up and the extra cash payments companies give you, and pretending you used that cash to buy more.
terms.analogy: Your apple tree grows bigger and also drops apples. Total return counts the bigger tree plus planting the dropped apples.
terms.precise: Price return plus dividends, compounded. For the S&P 500 dividends add about 1.5 to 2 percent a year, so leaving them out makes the benchmark easier to beat than it really is.

terms.simple: The thing you compare against. Ours is the S&P 500: if we cannot beat simply holding it, our strategy is not worth the effort.
terms.analogy: The time to beat in a race. Running fast means nothing unless you know what fast is.
terms.precise: A passive reference portfolio. Ours is SPY buy-and-hold with dividends and no costs, measured over exactly the same dates as each strategy. Defined in DEC-0006.

terms.simple: Long means you own something and win if its price goes up. Short means you bet against it and win if its price goes down.
terms.analogy: Long is buying a toy hoping it becomes rare. Short is borrowing a friend's toy, selling it now, and planning to buy it back cheaper later to give back.
terms.precise: A positive weight is a long position, a negative weight a short. In FX every position is long one currency and short another.

terms.simple: How much of your money is in each thing you hold.
terms.analogy: How you split your pocket money between sweets, stickers and saving.
terms.precise: The position in an asset as a fraction of capital. Strategies in this repo only output target weights; the backtester turns them into returns.

terms.simple: Using borrowed money to make your bets bigger. Wins get bigger, and so do losses.
terms.analogy: Riding a bike downhill. You go faster, and falling hurts more.
terms.precise: Gross exposure above 100% of capital. Volatility targeting in our backtester can lever a calm strategy up to 4 times to compare it with stocks at equal risk.
terms.risk: Losses grow as fast as gains, and borrowed money must be repaid even if the trade fails. Past a point, more leverage lowers long-run growth and can end in a margin call or liquidation.

terms.simple: Changing what you hold back to the plan, every week or month.
terms.analogy: Tidying your room on Sundays so it matches how you like it, even if it got messy during the week.
terms.precise: Trading to bring actual weights back to target weights on a schedule. More frequent rebalancing follows the signal more closely and costs more.

terms.simple: How much buying and selling a strategy does.
terms.analogy: How many times you swap your trading cards in a year. Each swap has a small fee.
terms.precise: The sum of absolute weight changes. A turnover of 12 a year means trading the whole portfolio about once a month.

terms.simple: The small gap between the price you can buy at and the price you can sell at. That gap is a cost every time you trade.
terms.analogy: A currency exchange booth at the airport buys dollars from you a bit cheaper than it sells them. The difference is how it makes money.
terms.precise: The difference between the best ask and the best bid. For major G10 pairs it is around 0.5 to 2 basis points for institutions, more for retail.

terms.simple: Everything it costs to make a trade: the spread, fees and moving the price against yourself.
terms.analogy: The delivery fee on every online order. One order is fine, a hundred small orders add up.
terms.precise: We charge a fixed cost per unit of notional traded (1 basis point by default) and test at double that in our 11 tests. Real costs also include financing markups and slippage.

terms.simple: One hundredth of one percent. 100 basis points is 1%.
terms.analogy: If 1% is a dollar, a basis point is one cent.
terms.precise: 0.01%, or 0.0001 as a fraction. Used for small numbers like costs and interest rate changes.

terms.simple: Something that moves up or down by chance each day, so yesterday's move tells you nothing about tomorrow's.
terms.analogy: Flipping a coin to decide whether to step left or right. Where you go next has nothing to do with where you came from.
terms.precise: A process whose changes are unpredictable. Meese and Rogoff (1983) found exchange rates are hard to forecast better than a random walk, which sets the bar for any currency strategy.

terms.simple: The idea that prices already include everything people know, so you cannot consistently beat the market without taking extra risk.
terms.analogy: If a shop had a hidden discount, so many people would find it that it would be gone in minutes.
terms.precise: The efficient market hypothesis: prices reflect available information, so predictable excess returns either compensate for risk or do not exist after costs.

terms.simple: The idea that markets have chances to win now and then, but they shrink once lots of people notice them.
terms.analogy: A secret fishing spot. It is great until your friends tell their friends.
terms.precise: Profit opportunities exist, attract capital and decay (Neely, Weller and Ulrich, 2009). Consistent with published FX factors losing most of their returns after publication.

terms.simple: Extra money you get paid for taking a risk most people do not want.
terms.analogy: Getting paid more for a job that is sometimes unpleasant. The extra pay is there because someone has to do it.
terms.precise: Expected return in excess of the risk-free rate, earned for bearing risk that cannot be diversified away. One explanation for carry returns (Lustig, Roussanov and Verdelhan, 2011).

terms.simple: Making money with no risk by buying something cheap in one place and selling it for more somewhere else at the same time.
terms.analogy: Buying a sticker for 10 cents at one table and selling it for 20 cents at the next table, right away.
terms.precise: A riskless profit from price differences. Real arbitrage opportunities are rare and close fast.

terms.simple: Things that have been going up tend to keep going up for a while, and things going down keep going down.
terms.analogy: A ball rolling downhill keeps rolling for a bit before it slows down.
terms.precise: Time-series momentum: an asset's own past return predicts its future return (Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen, 2012). Cross-sectional momentum: past winners beat past losers. Tested in HYP-0002.

terms.simple: When something moves far from normal, it tends to come back toward normal.
terms.analogy: A stretched rubber band snaps back.
terms.precise: A tendency for deviations from a long-run level to shrink over time. PPP deviations mean revert slowly; our commodity gap strategy bets on a faster kind of catch-up.

terms.simple: When economic news, like how many jobs were created, comes out very different from what experts expected.
terms.analogy: Expecting a B on a test and getting an A or a D. The surprise, not the grade, is what changes your mood.
terms.precise: The actual value of a data release minus the consensus forecast, usually scaled by its standard deviation. Surprises move currencies within minutes (Andersen, Bollerslev, Diebold and Vega, 2003). See HYP-0004.

terms.simple: The net amount people are buying or selling. More buyers than sellers pushes the price up.
terms.analogy: If everyone at school suddenly wants the same sneakers, their price goes up, whatever the reason.
terms.precise: Signed transaction volume. Explains a large share of daily exchange rate moves (Evans and Lyons, 2002). Mostly not available to us for free.

terms.simple: A period when markets behave in a particular way, like calm years, crisis years, or years of high interest rates.
terms.analogy: Seasons. What works in summer, like shorts, does not work in winter.
terms.precise: A stretch of time with distinct statistical behaviour. Strategies that only work in one regime are fragile. Our era test checks three regimes separately.

terms.simple: When a way of making money stops working because too many people started doing it.
terms.analogy: A shortcut through the park is fast until everyone uses it and it gets crowded.
terms.precise: The erosion of a strategy's excess return as capital crowds in. Published equity anomalies lose about 58% after publication (McLean and Pontiff, 2016); published FX factors turned negative (Hutchinson et al., 2022).

terms.simple: How much money you made or lost, as a percent of what you started with.
terms.analogy: If you plant 10 seeds and end up with 11 plants, your return is 10%.
terms.precise: The percentage change in value over a period. We work with daily returns net of costs.

terms.simple: The average yearly growth, as if your money grew by the same percent every year.
terms.analogy: If a plant grew from 10 cm to 40 cm in two years, CAGR says how much it grew each year on average, counting that it got bigger each year.
terms.precise: Compound annual growth rate: final value over starting value, to the power one over the number of years, minus one.

terms.simple: How bumpy the ride is. High volatility means big ups and downs.
terms.analogy: A calm lake versus a stormy sea. Both might get you across, one is a lot scarier.
terms.precise: The standard deviation of returns, annualised by multiplying daily volatility by the square root of 252. The S&P 500 has run at about 15 to 19% a year.

terms.simple: Making bets bigger when markets are calm and smaller when they are wild, so the ride stays about equally bumpy.
terms.analogy: Driving faster on an empty straight road and slower on a winding one, so the trip feels the same.
terms.precise: Scaling positions by target volatility over recent realised volatility, using only past data. Lets us compare a calm currency strategy with stocks at the same risk.

terms.simple: How much money a strategy makes for each unit of bumpiness. Higher is better. Around 0.5 is what the stock market has done.
terms.analogy: Points scored per foul. A player who scores a lot but fouls all the time might not be your best player.
terms.precise: Mean return divided by the standard deviation of returns, annualised by the square root of 252. We use a zero risk-free rate for both strategy and benchmark.

terms.simple: Like the Sharpe ratio, but it only counts the bad bumps, the days you lose money.
terms.analogy: Judging a rollercoaster only by how scary the drops are, not by the climbs.
terms.precise: Mean return over downside deviation (root mean square of negative returns), annualised.

terms.simple: How far you have fallen from your highest point. The max drawdown is the worst fall ever.
terms.analogy: Climbing a hill and sliding back down part of it. The drawdown is how far you slid.
terms.precise: Equity divided by its running peak, minus one. The S&P 500 fell about 55% from 2007 to 2009.

terms.simple: Yearly growth divided by the worst fall. It asks: how much did you earn for the worst pain you went through?
terms.analogy: How good the holiday was compared with the worst day of it.
terms.precise: CAGR divided by the absolute maximum drawdown.

terms.simple: The share of days the strategy made money.
terms.analogy: How often you win at a game. You can win rarely and still come out ahead if your wins are big.
terms.precise: Fraction of non-zero daily returns that are positive.

terms.simple: How much two things move together, from minus 1 (always opposite) through 0 (unrelated) to plus 1 (always together).
terms.analogy: Ice cream sales and sunny days have a high correlation. Ice cream sales and your shoe size have none.
terms.precise: Pearson correlation of daily returns. A strategy with low or negative correlation with the S&P 500 could improve a stock portfolio even if it earns less.

terms.simple: How much a strategy moves when the stock market moves. A beta of 1 moves just like the market, 0 ignores it.
terms.analogy: A small boat tied to a big ship. Beta is how much the small boat rocks when the ship rocks.
terms.precise: Covariance with the benchmark divided by the benchmark's variance.

terms.simple: Not putting all your eggs in one basket, so one bad thing does not ruin everything.
terms.analogy: Bringing an umbrella and sunglasses. Whatever the weather, one of them helps.
terms.precise: Combining assets that are not perfectly correlated lowers portfolio volatility for the same expected return. The idea behind HYP-0007.

terms.simple: How much more (or less) the strategy made than the benchmark.
terms.analogy: How many seconds faster than the time to beat.
terms.precise: Strategy CAGR minus benchmark CAGR over the same dates. Only meaningful at comparable risk.

terms.simple: How steadily the strategy beats the benchmark, not just by how much.
terms.analogy: A runner who beats the record by a little every single race versus one who wins big once and loses the rest.
terms.precise: Mean active return (strategy minus benchmark) divided by its standard deviation (tracking error), annualised.

terms.simple: Lots of small wins and a few huge losses.
terms.analogy: Selling lemonade every day and then once a year a storm knocks over the whole stand.
terms.precise: A return distribution with a long left tail. Carry trades are negatively skewed (Daniel, Hodrick and Lu, 2017), which a Sharpe ratio alone hides.

terms.simple: Very big moves happen more often than a simple bell curve says they should.
terms.analogy: Weather forecasts that say a huge storm happens once in a hundred years, and then two hit in a decade.
terms.precise: Excess kurtosis. The deflated Sharpe ratio corrects for it, because fat tails make an observed Sharpe less reliable.

terms.simple: How expensive trading would have to be before the strategy stops making money.
terms.analogy: If you earn 5 dollars a week from your lemonade stand, the break-even cost is how high the rent can go before you earn nothing.
terms.precise: Average gross daily return divided by average daily turnover, in basis points. It should be several times real trading costs.

terms.simple: The number a strategy uses to decide what to buy or sell, like a hint about the future.
terms.analogy: Dark clouds are a signal that it might rain. They are not always right, but they help.
terms.precise: A forecast score per instrument per day, before it is turned into weights. Strategies here can expose their signal so we can measure its information coefficient.

terms.simple: How good the signal is at guessing what happens next. 0 means useless, 1 means perfect. In currency markets, 0.03 is already decent.
terms.analogy: How often the weather forecaster is right, beyond what you would get by guessing.
terms.precise: The rank correlation between the signal and the forward return across instruments on each date, averaged over time. We report it at 1, 5, 21 and 63 days ahead (IC decay).

terms.simple: How long a signal's hint stays useful. Some hints are only good for a day, some for months.
terms.analogy: A weather forecast for tomorrow is good, one for next month much less so. Some clues fade fast, some slowly.
terms.precise: The information coefficient measured at several horizons. Where it peaks suggests how often to trade. Rising IC with horizon means trade slower.

terms.simple: Pretending to run a strategy in the past to see how it would have done.
terms.analogy: Replaying an old football match with your new tactics on a video game. Useful, but the real match can go differently.
terms.precise: A historical simulation. Ours holds today's decision from tomorrow, charges costs, and credits carry. A backtest is evidence, never proof.

terms.simple: Accidentally using information from the future in a backtest. It makes results look much better than they could ever be.
terms.analogy: Betting on a race after you already saw the results.
terms.precise: Using data in a decision that was not available at the time, such as same-day closes, revised macro data, or full-sample estimates. Our backtester holds weights from the next day to prevent the most common form.

terms.simple: Only looking at the winners that are still around and forgetting the ones that disappeared.
terms.analogy: Saying all old buildings were built well, because the badly built ones already fell down.
terms.precise: Excluding assets that died, were delisted or redenominated. Small for G10 currencies, large for crypto and emerging markets.

terms.simple: Tuning a strategy so it fits the past perfectly, including the random parts, so it fails in the future.
terms.analogy: Memorising last year's test answers instead of learning the subject. Great score on last year's test, bad score on this year's.
terms.precise: Fitting noise rather than signal. The more settings and ideas tried, the more likely the best one is overfit. Countered by deflated statistics, holdout data and sensitivity tests.

terms.simple: Trying so many ideas that one of them looks great just by luck.
terms.analogy: If 100 people each flip a coin 10 times, someone will get 9 heads. That person is not a coin-flipping genius.
terms.precise: Inflated significance from testing many hypotheses on the same data. Harvey, Liu and Zhu (2016) argue for a t-statistic hurdle near 3 instead of 2.

terms.simple: Data you did not look at while designing the strategy, kept aside to test it fairly.
terms.analogy: A practice test the teacher keeps hidden until the end, so you cannot study the exact questions.
terms.precise: Observations excluded from model selection. Our tests treat the last five years as the hardest test and check three separate eras.

terms.simple: A Sharpe ratio that is made harder to pass the more ideas we tried. It gives the chance, from 0 to 1, that the strategy is truly better than nothing. We want at least 0.95.
terms.analogy: If you take one shot and score, that is impressive. If you take 100 shots and score once, less so. This adjusts for the number of shots.
terms.precise: The probability that the true Sharpe exceeds the best Sharpe expected from N unskilled trials, adjusted for skew, kurtosis and sample length (Bailey and Lopez de Prado, 2014).

terms.simple: Making many slightly jumbled copies of history to see how much a result could change by chance.
terms.analogy: Shuffling a deck of cards many times to see how often a good hand turns up.
terms.precise: Resampling the data with replacement. We use a moving block bootstrap (21-day blocks, 1,000 resamples) so calm and stormy stretches stay together.

terms.simple: A range where the true answer probably is. A 95% range means we would expect the true value inside it 95 times out of 100.
terms.analogy: Saying the bus will come between 8:05 and 8:15 instead of exactly 8:10.
terms.precise: An interval estimate. One of our 11 tests asks whether the 95% bootstrap interval for the Sharpe ratio lies entirely above zero.

terms.simple: Running a fake version of the strategy that cannot possibly know anything, to check the real one does better.
terms.analogy: In medicine, some people get a sugar pill. If they get better as often as people on the real pill, the pill does nothing.
terms.precise: We keep the strategy's positions but shift them to random dates 500 times, keeping size and trading but destroying timing. The real strategy should beat at least 95% of these.

terms.simple: The chance of seeing a result this good if the strategy was actually useless. Small is good. Below 0.05 is the usual bar.
terms.analogy: How surprised you should be. A friend guessing a coin flip once is not surprising. Ten times in a row is.
terms.precise: The probability, under a null hypothesis, of a statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. In the placebo test it is the share of random-date copies that do as well.

terms.simple: How many times bigger a result is than the noise around it. Above 2 is the usual bar; finance researchers now ask for 3.
terms.analogy: Hearing a friend's voice across a noisy room. The louder their voice compared with the noise, the surer you are it is them.
terms.precise: An estimate divided by its standard error. Overlapping return windows make it look bigger than it really is.

terms.simple: An estimate of how likely it is that the best strategy in our tests will do worse than average on new data.
terms.analogy: How often the student who topped the practice test ends up below average on the real one.
terms.precise: From combinatorially symmetric cross-validation (Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado and Zhu, 2016). On our roadmap.

terms.simple: Trying to guess where a price goes next by looking only at its past prices and trading volume on a chart.
terms.analogy: Like guessing tomorrow's weather only from the last few days of weather, without looking at the clouds or the season.
terms.precise: Forecasting from past prices and volume alone. A review of 95 modern studies found 56 reported profits, but many had problems with data snooping, rules picked after the fact and cost estimates [@park2007]. In currencies, simple rules made money in the 1970s and 1980s and much less after the early 1990s [@neely2009]. It is widespread among FX professionals [@menkhoff2007].

terms.simple: A little drawing that shows four prices for one stretch of time: where the price started, where it ended, the highest it went and the lowest it went.
terms.analogy: Like a thermometer with a mark for the morning temperature, the evening temperature, and the hottest and coldest moments of the day.
terms.precise: A chart mark for one period showing open, high, low and close. The box (body) spans open to close and the lines (wicks) reach the high and low. Popularised in the West by Nison (1991) [@nison1991]. A candle is just a picture of four numbers; it holds no information that the four numbers do not.

terms.simple: The four prices for a time period: open, high, low and close.
terms.analogy: Like a short diary of a day: how it started, the best moment, the worst moment and how it ended.
terms.precise: Open, high, low and close for one period (a minute, an hour, a day). Bar charts and candlestick charts draw the same four numbers in different shapes. Note that FX has no single official open or close, so different data vendors give slightly different daily bars.

terms.simple: The thick box part of a candlestick. It shows how far the price moved from start to finish.
terms.analogy: Like the distance between where you started your walk and where you ended up, ignoring the detours.
terms.precise: The span between open and close. It is usually filled or coloured red when the close is below the open (a bearish candle) and hollow or green when the close is above the open (a bullish candle).

terms.simple: The thin lines sticking out of the top and bottom of a candle. They show the highest and lowest prices that were reached.
terms.analogy: Like the farthest you wandered off the path during a walk, even if you came back.
terms.precise: Also called shadows. The upper wick runs from the top of the body to the high, the lower wick from the bottom of the body to the low. Long wicks mean the price visited a level and then moved away from it within the period.

terms.simple: A bullish candle closed higher than it opened. A bearish candle closed lower than it opened.
terms.analogy: Like a day that ended better than it began, or worse than it began.
terms.precise: Bullish: close above open. Bearish: close below open. The words describe what already happened in that period, not what will happen next.

terms.simple: A candle where the price ended almost exactly where it started, so the body is a thin line.
terms.analogy: Like a tug of war that ends with the rope in the same place it started.
terms.precise: A candle whose open and close are nearly equal, read by chartists as indecision. There is no agreed threshold for 'nearly equal'. A test of candlestick rules on Dow Jones stocks from 1992 to 2002 found no value [@marshall2005].

terms.simple: A candle with a small body and long wicks on both sides.
terms.analogy: Like a spinning top that wobbles a lot but stays in about the same place.
terms.precise: Small body, upper and lower wicks both longer than the body. Chartists read it as indecision, like a doji with a slightly larger body. We know of no large test that finds it predicts direction.

terms.simple: A candle with a big body and almost no wicks: the price moved one way the whole time.
terms.analogy: Like a runner who sprints in a straight line from start to finish without slowing or turning.
terms.precise: A candle whose open is at or near one extreme and close at or near the other. Chartists read it as strong pressure in one direction. A test on Dow Jones stocks from 1992 to 2002 found candlestick strategies had no value [@marshall2005].

terms.simple: A candle with a small body at the top and a long wick below it, appearing after the price has been falling.
terms.analogy: Like a ball that is thrown hard at the floor and bounces most of the way back up.
terms.precise: Small body near the high, lower wick at least about twice the body, little or no upper wick, after a decline. Chartists read it as a possible turn up. A test of candlestick strategies on Dow Jones stocks from 1992 to 2002 found no value [@marshall2005].

terms.simple: The same shape as a hammer, but it shows up after the price has been rising.
terms.analogy: The same shape can mean different things depending on where you see it, like a raised hand in class or at a bus stop.
terms.precise: Small body near the high with a long lower wick, after an advance. Chartists read it as a possible turn down. That one shape gets opposite names by context is a warning sign about how flexible these rules are; the Dow Jones test found candlestick strategies had no value [@marshall2005].

terms.simple: A candle with a small body at the bottom and a long wick above it, after the price has been rising.
terms.analogy: Like a rocket that shoots up and then falls back down to where it started.
terms.precise: Small body near the low, long upper wick, after an advance. Chartists read it as a possible turn down. As with other candles, the Dow Jones test found no value [@marshall2005].

terms.simple: The same shape as a shooting star, but it shows up after the price has been falling.
terms.analogy: An upside down hammer.
terms.precise: Small body near the low and a long upper wick, after a decline. Read by chartists as a possible turn up. No large test we know of supports it as a reliable signal.

terms.simple: Two candles where the second one's body is bigger than the first and points the other way, like it swallowed the first one.
terms.analogy: Like a big wave that washes over the sandcastle the small wave built.
terms.precise: A two-candle pattern: a bullish engulfing is a bearish candle followed by a bullish candle whose body covers the first body; bearish engulfing is the reverse. Results are mixed: a test on Dow Jones stocks found no value [@marshall2005], while a study of Taiwan stocks found three bullish two-day patterns profitable [@lu2012].

terms.simple: Two candles where the second one is small and fits inside the body of the first one.
terms.analogy: Like a baby tucked inside its mother. Harami is Japanese for pregnant.
terms.precise: A large body followed by a small body contained within it, read by chartists as a possible pause or turn. The evidence is the same as for other candle patterns: no value in the Dow Jones test [@marshall2005].

terms.simple: A three-candle pattern: a big down candle, a small candle, then a big up candle. Chartists say it signals a bottom.
terms.analogy: Like the morning star that appears just before sunrise, after the dark night.
terms.precise: A long bearish candle, a small-bodied candle that gaps or sits lower, then a long bullish candle closing well into the first body. Caginalp and Laurent (1998) found three-day candlestick patterns had predictive power in S&P 500 stocks from 1992 to 1996 [@caginalp1998a]; a test on Dow Jones stocks from 1992 to 2002 found no value [@marshall2005].

terms.simple: The upside-down version of a morning star: a big up candle, a small candle, then a big down candle. Chartists say it signals a top.
terms.analogy: Like the evening star that shows up as the day ends.
terms.precise: A long bullish candle, a small-bodied candle, then a long bearish candle closing well into the first body. Same evidence as the morning star: support in one sample [@caginalp1998a], none in another [@marshall2005].

terms.simple: Three up candles in a row, each closing higher than the one before.
terms.analogy: Like three steps up a staircase.
terms.precise: Three consecutive long bullish candles, each opening within the prior body and closing near its high. Chartists read it as strong buying. Three up periods in a row also happen often by chance in a random walk; a rule needs testing against that baseline.

terms.simple: Three down candles in a row, each closing lower than the one before.
terms.analogy: Like three steps down a staircase.
terms.precise: The bearish mirror of three white soldiers. The same caution applies: streaks are common in random data [@tversky1971].

terms.simple: A chart shape with three peaks where the middle one is the tallest, like a head between two shoulders. Chartists say it means the price will fall.
terms.analogy: Like seeing a face in the clouds: you can usually find one if you look for it.
terms.precise: A pattern of three peaks with the middle highest, and a 'neckline' through the troughs. On daily dollar exchange rates from 1973 to 1994, Chang and Osler (1999) found the rule was profitable but beaten by simpler trading rules [@chang1999]. Lo, Mamaysky and Wang (2000) found such patterns carry a little information in US stocks [@lo2000].

terms.simple: A double top is when the price climbs to the same high twice and fails both times. A double bottom is the same at a low.
terms.analogy: Like a ball that hits the same ceiling twice before you give up throwing it.
terms.precise: Two peaks (or troughs) at a similar level separated by a pullback. Chartists read it as a reversal once price breaks the level between them. Algorithmic tests find these shapes have at most a small amount of information [@lo2000].

terms.simple: Price levels where people believe a falling price tends to stop (support) or a rising price tends to stop (resistance).
terms.analogy: Like a floor and a ceiling in a room: the ball bounces off them, until one day it breaks through.
terms.precise: Levels where buying or selling interest is thought to gather. In FX there is some real support: levels published by six firms helped predict intraday trend stops from 1996 to 1998 [@osler2000], and customer stop-loss and take-profit orders cluster at round numbers, which can explain why such levels matter [@osler2003].

terms.simple: A straight line drawn along the lows (or highs) of a chart to show which way the price has been heading.
terms.analogy: Like drawing a line along the edge of a hill to see how steep it is.
terms.precise: A line through two or more swing lows or highs. Which points to use is a choice, so two people can draw different trendlines on the same chart. This freedom makes trendline rules hard to test fairly.

terms.simple: When the price moves past a level it had stopped at before, like support or resistance.
terms.analogy: Like water finally spilling over the top of a dam.
terms.precise: A move through a prior high, low or range boundary. Channel breakout rules are one of the simple trend-following rules that made money in FX before the 1990s [@neely2009]. Osler (2003) found that trends tend to speed up after rates cross round numbers, consistent with stop-loss orders being triggered [@osler2003].

terms.simple: When the price pokes past a level but then quickly comes back.
terms.analogy: Like someone stepping out the door, feeling the rain and stepping back inside.
terms.precise: A break of a level that reverses within a short time. Osler (2003) found that rates tend to reverse at round numbers, where take-profit orders cluster, so not every break of a level should be expected to continue [@osler2003].

terms.simple: An empty space on a chart where the price jumped from one level to another without trading in between.
terms.analogy: Like skipping several stairs in one jump.
terms.precise: A period whose range does not overlap the previous period's range. FX trades around the clock on weekdays, so gaps appear mostly over weekends or after sudden news. A gap means a stop order can fill far from its level.

terms.simple: Lines drawn at certain fractions (like 38.2%, 50% and 61.8%) of a past move, where some traders expect the price to pause.
terms.analogy: Like believing a bouncing ball will always stop at the same fraction of its last bounce because of a famous number.
terms.precise: Levels at Fibonacci ratios of a prior swing. We found no peer-reviewed large-sample study showing these levels predict turning points better than other levels; they may matter a little only because many people watch them. The general technical analysis literature is cautious [@park2007].

terms.simple: The average price over the last few days, recalculated each day, so it smooths out the wiggles.
terms.analogy: Like your average score over your last ten games, updated after every game.
terms.precise: The mean of the last N prices, either equally weighted (simple) or with more weight on recent prices (exponential). It always lags the price, because it is built from the past.

terms.simple: A rule to buy when a short average climbs above a long average, and sell when it drops below.
terms.analogy: Like deciding a hill is going up once your last few steps are higher than your last fifty steps.
terms.precise: A trend rule comparing a short and a long moving average. In FX such rules earned excess returns in the 1970s and 1980s that faded after the early 1990s [@neely2009]. On the Dow Jones, the best rule from Brock, Lakonishok and LeBaron's (1992) sample did not keep working from 1987 to 1996 [@brock1992; @sullivan1999].

terms.simple: A number from 0 to 100 that compares recent up moves to recent down moves. High is said to mean 'overbought', low 'oversold'.
terms.analogy: Like a speedometer that shows how fast the price has been climbing compared with falling.
terms.precise: An oscillator, usually over 14 periods: 100 minus 100 divided by (1 plus average gain over average loss). Readings above 70 or below 30 are common thresholds. 'Overbought' does not mean due to fall; in trending markets RSI can stay high for a long time. Evidence for RSI rules is part of the mixed technical analysis literature [@park2007].

terms.simple: A tool that subtracts a slow moving average from a fast one to show whether a trend is speeding up or slowing down.
terms.analogy: Like comparing how fast you walked in the last minute with how fast you walked over the last ten.
terms.precise: Moving average convergence divergence: the 12-period exponential average minus the 26-period one, with a 9-period average of that difference as a signal line. It is a trend rule built from moving averages, with the same lag and the same mixed evidence.

terms.simple: Lines drawn above and below a moving average at a distance that grows when the price is jumpy and shrinks when it is calm.
terms.analogy: Like the lane lines on a road that get wider when the traffic is swerving more.
terms.precise: A moving average plus and minus a multiple (often 2) of the rolling standard deviation. Touching a band is used by some as a reversal signal and by others as a breakout signal, which shows the rule does not by itself say which.

terms.simple: Trading by reading the shapes the price makes on a chart, usually without other indicators.
terms.analogy: Like reading someone's mood from their face instead of asking them.
terms.precise: A discretionary style built on candles, levels and patterns. Because rules are rarely written down, it is hard to test, and we found no large-sample evidence for it as a whole. When written as rules, tests fall under the technical analysis literature [@park2007].

terms.simple: Many traders put their orders at tidy prices like 1.1000 instead of 1.1037, so lots of orders pile up there.
terms.analogy: Like how prices in shops end in .99 or .00 more than any other number.
terms.precise: In customer order books at a large FX dealer, take-profit orders clustered at round numbers and stop-loss orders just beyond them, which helps explain why trends often reverse at round numbers and speed up after crossing them [@osler2003].

terms.simple: A shortcut in how our brains think that makes us get the same kind of thing wrong again and again.
terms.analogy: Like a bathroom scale that always reads two kilos light. It is not random; it is wrong in the same direction every time.
terms.precise: A systematic departure from what probability or logic would say. Tversky and Kahneman (1974) showed that rules of thumb for judging chances, such as representativeness, availability and anchoring, lead to predictable errors [@tversky1974]. Behavioural finance studies how these errors show up in prices and trading [@barberis2003].

terms.simple: Thinking you know more, or are better at something, than you really are.
terms.analogy: Like most drivers saying they are better than the average driver, which cannot be true for most of them.
terms.precise: Overestimating the precision of one's information or one's skill. Barber and Odean (2001) found men traded 45% more than women and cut their net returns by 2.65 percentage points a year against 1.72 for women, consistent with overconfidence [@barber2001].

terms.simple: Losing something hurts more than winning the same thing feels good.
terms.analogy: Losing a ten pound note hurts more than finding one cheers you up.
terms.precise: Kahneman and Tversky (1979) found the value function is generally steeper for losses than for gains [@kahneman1979]. Later work put a number on how much steeper; we have not yet checked those estimates.

terms.simple: A theory that says people judge choices by gains and losses from where they are now, and hate losses more than they like gains.
terms.analogy: Like judging a test score by whether it beat your last one, not by the score itself.
terms.precise: Kahneman and Tversky (1979): outcomes are valued relative to a reference point, with a value function concave for gains, convex for losses and steeper for losses, and with decision weights in place of probabilities [@kahneman1979].

terms.simple: The habit of selling winning trades too early and holding losing trades too long, hoping they come back.
terms.analogy: Like leaving a party you are enjoying, but staying at one you hate because you already paid for the ticket.
terms.precise: The tendency to realise gains more readily than losses [@shefrin1985]. In 10,000 US brokerage accounts, Odean (1998) found a strong preference for realising winners rather than losers, and later returns did not justify it [@odean1998]. Among retail traders, access to a social trading network nearly doubled the effect [@heimer2016].

terms.simple: Giving too much weight to what just happened and too little to everything before.
terms.analogy: Like thinking summer will never end after three hot days, even though you remember last winter.
terms.precise: Overweighting recent observations when forming expectations. Investor surveys show expected returns track recent past returns, while being strongly negatively related to model-based expected returns [@greenwood2014].

terms.simple: Expecting what has been happening to keep happening.
terms.analogy: Like expecting a growing puppy to become the size of a horse because it doubled in size this year.
terms.precise: Forming expectations by projecting recent trends forward. Greenwood and Shleifer (2014) found investor return expectations move with past returns but are strongly negatively related to model-based expected returns [@greenwood2014]. De Bondt and Thaler (1985) found past extreme losers later beat past extreme winners in US stocks, consistent with overreaction [@debondt1985].

terms.simple: Noticing and believing things that agree with what you already think, and ignoring things that do not.
terms.analogy: Like only reading reviews that praise the film you already decided to see.
terms.precise: The tendency to seek, interpret and remember evidence in ways that favour existing beliefs [@nickerson1998]. For traders it shows up as reading news that supports an open position and dismissing news against it.

terms.simple: After something happens, feeling like you knew it would happen all along.
terms.analogy: Like saying 'I knew that team would win' only after the match is over.
terms.precise: Knowing an outcome makes people judge it as more predictable than it was [@fischhoff1975]. Charts make this worse: every past turning point looks obvious afterwards.

terms.simple: Thinking that after many reds on a roulette wheel, black is 'due'. It is not; the wheel does not remember.
terms.analogy: Like thinking a coin feels guilty after five heads and will try to land tails.
terms.precise: Believing independent events self-correct in the short run, a form of the 'law of small numbers' [@tversky1971; @tversky1974]. For trading: after a run of losses, the next trade of an independent strategy is not more likely to win.

terms.simple: Believing someone who has just had several wins in a row is more likely to win again.
terms.analogy: Like a basketball fan who wants the ball passed to whoever just scored three in a row.
terms.precise: Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky (1985) argued the hot hand in basketball was a misperception of random streaks [@gilovich1985]. Miller and Sanjurjo (2018) showed that study's measure was biased, and that once corrected its conclusion reverses [@miller2018]. The lesson for us: judging streaks is hard, and short track records say little.

terms.simple: The mistake of thinking a few results tell you the whole story.
terms.analogy: Like tasting one grape and deciding the whole vineyard is sour.
terms.precise: Tversky and Kahneman (1971): people expect small samples to look like the population they come from, so they read too much into short runs of data [@tversky1971]. A month of trading results is a small sample.

terms.simple: Getting stuck on the first number you hear, even if it has nothing to do with the question.
terms.analogy: Like a shop showing a huge 'original price' so the sale price feels cheap.
terms.precise: Estimates are pulled toward an initial value, even an arbitrary one [@tversky1974]. Traders often anchor on their entry price, which has no effect on where the market goes next.

terms.simple: Judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind.
terms.analogy: Like being scared of sharks after a shark film, though you are far more likely to be hurt driving to the beach.
terms.precise: Frequency or probability is judged by ease of recall [@tversky1974]. Vivid stories of big trading wins are easy to recall; quiet account closures are not.

terms.simple: Judging something by how much it looks like a typical example, and forgetting how common it actually is.
terms.analogy: Like assuming a quiet person who loves books must be a librarian, though there are far more quiet salespeople than librarians.
terms.precise: Judging probability by similarity to a stereotype while neglecting base rates and sample size [@tversky1974]. A chart that 'looks like' a famous pattern is judged likely to behave like it.

terms.simple: Believing you can influence things that are really down to chance.
terms.analogy: Like people throwing dice harder when they want a high number.
terms.precise: Langer (1975) showed people act as if they have more control over chance outcomes when chance tasks include features of skill tasks, such as competition, choice, familiarity or involvement [@langer1975]. Watching screens and drawing lines can feel like control over prices that we do not have.

terms.simple: Sticking with something because you already put time or money into it, even when stopping is the better choice.
terms.analogy: Like finishing a terrible meal because you paid for it, so you lose your money and your evening.
terms.precise: Letting unrecoverable past costs affect present choices [@arkes1985]. The money already lost on a trade is gone either way; only the expected value from here matters.

terms.simple: Putting more and more into a losing plan because you do not want to admit it was wrong.
terms.analogy: Like digging a hole deeper to get out of it.
terms.precise: Staw (1976) found people who were responsible for a failing decision put more resources into it than people who were not [@staw1976]. In trading this looks like adding to a losing position without a rule that says to.

terms.simple: Doing what everyone else is doing because they are doing it.
terms.analogy: Like choosing the busy restaurant over the empty one without looking at the menu.
terms.precise: Banerjee (1992) showed it can be rational for each person to copy others, yet the group as a whole can end up wrong [@banerjee1992]. Crowded trades can unwind suddenly when many leave at once [@brunnermeier2008].

terms.simple: Jumping into a trade because everyone seems to be making money and you feel left behind.
terms.analogy: Like buying a toy only because all your friends have it.
terms.precise: A popular term, not an academic one. The nearest evidence: individual investors are net buyers of stocks that grab attention, such as those in the news or with extreme one-day moves [@barber2008].

terms.simple: Trading bigger or more often right after a loss to try to win the money back fast.
terms.analogy: Like a player who loses a game and immediately bets double to 'get even'.
terms.precise: A trader's term, not an academic one. The closest studied effect is the break-even effect: after a loss, people take more risk when it offers a chance to get back to even [@thaler1990].

terms.simple: When strong feelings after wins or losses make you trade badly.
terms.analogy: Like a pinball machine that stops working properly when shaken.
terms.precise: Poker slang for emotional decision making. In a small study of day traders, those with stronger emotional reactions to gains and losses had worse results [@lo2005].

terms.simple: Taking bigger risks with money you just won, as if it is not really yours.
terms.analogy: Like spending birthday money more freely than money you earned.
terms.precise: Thaler and Johnson (1990) found that after a gain people are more willing to take risks, treating winnings as 'house money' [@thaler1990]. Money is money: a profit already in the account is as real as the deposit.

terms.simple: Putting money into separate boxes in your head and treating each box differently, even though money is all the same.
terms.analogy: Like refusing to touch your 'holiday jar' while paying interest on a credit card.
terms.precise: Thaler (1985): people code, categorise and evaluate outcomes in separate mental accounts rather than by total wealth [@thaler1985]. Judging each trade alone, instead of the whole account, is one form.

terms.simple: Making a different choice depending on how the same thing is described.
terms.analogy: Like a yoghurt that is '90% fat free' sounding better than one with '10% fat'.
terms.precise: Tversky and Kahneman (1981) showed choices reverse when the same outcomes are described as gains or as losses [@tversky1981]. A '60% win rate' and 'loses 4 times in 10' are the same fact.

terms.simple: Checking your results too often makes losses feel more frequent, so you get scared out of good long-term choices.
terms.analogy: Like weighing yourself every hour on a diet and panicking at every glass of water.
terms.precise: Benartzi and Thaler (1995): loss aversion plus frequent evaluation makes risky assets look worse, which can help explain the equity premium [@benartzi1995]. The more often a volatile strategy is checked, the more often it shows a loss.

terms.simple: Valuing something more just because you own it.
terms.analogy: Like refusing to sell your old bike for a price you would never pay to buy it.
terms.precise: Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler (1990) found that what owners ask to give up an object such as a mug greatly exceeds what buyers will pay, even in markets [@kahneman1990]. An open position can feel worth more than it is because it is ours.

terms.simple: Preferring to keep things as they are, even when a change would be better.
terms.analogy: Like always ordering the same meal because changing feels risky.
terms.precise: Samuelson and Zeckhauser (1988) found people choose the current option far more often than they would if it were not the default [@samuelson1988].

terms.simple: Making up a neat story to explain random events, and then believing the story.
terms.analogy: Like deciding your team lost because you wore the wrong socks.
terms.precise: Taleb's term for our need to fit a cause-and-effect story to sequences of facts, which makes the world seem more predictable than it is [@taleb2007]. Daily market commentary often explains moves after they happen.

terms.simple: Judging a decision only by how it turned out, instead of by whether it was a good choice at the time.
terms.analogy: Like praising someone for driving home drunk because they did not crash.
terms.precise: Baron and Hershey (1988) found people rated the same decision as better when it had a good outcome [@baron1988]. One trade's result says very little about the quality of the decision.

terms.simple: Trading too often, so costs and mistakes eat your money.
terms.analogy: Like checking the oven every minute: the cake does not bake faster and you let the heat out.
terms.precise: Barber and Odean (2000) found the US households that traded most earned 11.4% a year against 17.9% for the market, mostly because of costs [@barber2000].

terms.simple: Deciding how much money to put into each trade.
terms.analogy: Like deciding how big a slice of cake to take, knowing you might drop it.
terms.precise: Choosing trade size given the account size, the expected edge and the risk of the trade. It often matters more for survival than the entry rule. Common methods: fixed fraction of equity at risk, volatility scaling and fractions of Kelly [@carver2015; @thorp2008].

terms.simple: The most money you agree to lose on one trade if it goes wrong, often a small share of your account.
terms.analogy: Like only betting pocket money you can afford to lose, never your bus fare home.
terms.precise: The loss if the stop is hit, as a share of equity. The common '1 to 2 percent' rule has little direct large-sample evidence (see RES-0006), but the arithmetic is sound: small fixed fractions make a long losing streak survivable. Gaps can make the real loss larger than planned.

terms.simple: Risking the same small percentage of whatever your account is worth now on every trade.
terms.analogy: Like always eating a quarter of whatever cake is left: you never run out, though the slices get smaller.
terms.precise: Each position risks a fixed fraction f of current equity, so size shrinks after losses and grows after gains. In theory this avoids total ruin, though costs, minimum trade sizes and gaps still allow it in practice. The Kelly criterion is the growth-optimal choice of f for a known edge [@thorp2008].

terms.simple: A formula that tells you what share of your money to bet so it grows fastest over many bets, if you know your real chances.
terms.analogy: Like knowing exactly how hard to pedal uphill: too little and you crawl, too much and you burn out.
terms.precise: The fraction that maximises expected log wealth. For a bet paying b to 1 with win probability p, f = p minus (1 minus p) divided by b. For a continuous asset it is roughly expected excess return divided by variance. Derived by Kelly (1956) [@url-efa4ec7e]; its use in betting and markets is reviewed by Thorp [@thorp2008; @maclean2011]. It assumes the edge is known exactly, which it never is.

terms.simple: Betting only a part, like half, of what the Kelly formula says, to be safer.
terms.analogy: Like driving a bit under the speed limit because you are not sure how icy the road is.
terms.precise: Betting a fraction c of the Kelly amount. With a known edge, growth at c times Kelly is proportional to c times (2 minus c), so half Kelly keeps three quarters of the maximum growth, and twice Kelly gives zero growth. Betting below Kelly is much less harmful if the edge was overestimated [@maclean2011].

terms.simple: A number that says 'on most days, we should not lose more than this much'.
terms.analogy: Like a weather report saying 'there is only a 1 in 20 chance of more than 10 mm of rain', which tells you nothing about how bad that 1 day might be.
terms.precise: The loss level not exceeded with a given probability over a given horizon, for example 99% one-day VaR. It says nothing about how large losses are beyond that level and is not always subadditive, so combining positions can appear to raise it [@jorion2006; @artzner1999].

terms.simple: The average loss on the really bad days, the ones past the VaR line.
terms.analogy: If VaR says how deep the water usually gets, expected shortfall says how deep it is on average when it floods.
terms.precise: The expected loss given that the loss exceeds the VaR level, also called conditional VaR. It is a coherent risk measure [@acerbi2002; @artzner1999]. Bank market risk rules moved from VaR to expected shortfall in the Basel framework [@bcbs2019].

terms.simple: The chance of losing so much that you cannot keep trading.
terms.analogy: Like the chance a gambler runs out of chips before the night ends.
terms.precise: The probability that equity falls to a level where trading must stop. Classic gambler's ruin results show that with a fixed bet size even a favourable game has a positive ruin probability, and an unfavourable game ends in ruin with certainty given enough time [@feller1968]. Larger bets relative to capital raise it sharply.

terms.simple: The math showing that a player with less money, betting against a richer opponent in a fair or unfair game, will usually go broke eventually.
terms.analogy: Like playing tug of war against a team that never gets tired.
terms.precise: Results for a random walk with absorbing barriers: a player with finite capital in a game with zero or negative edge is ruined with probability 1 against an opponent with unlimited capital [@feller1968]. Martingale betting systems run into this.

terms.simple: How long it takes to climb back to your old best after a fall.
terms.analogy: Like how long it takes to get back to the top of the hill after sliding down.
terms.precise: The time from a peak in equity to the point where that peak is regained. For a random walk with positive drift, the expected maximum drawdown keeps growing with the time horizon, roughly like its logarithm; with zero drift it grows like the square root [@magdonismail2004]. Long stretches below a past peak are normal.

terms.simple: Money you must keep with your broker as a deposit when you trade with borrowed money.
terms.analogy: Like the deposit you pay to rent a bike: you get it back if you return the bike, and you lose it if you break it.
terms.precise: Collateral posted against a leveraged position. In the EU, retail CFD rules require initial margin of at least 3.33% for major currency pairs (30 to 1 leverage) [@url-46fb23ac]. In the US, the CFTC's 2010 rule has the National Futures Association set retail forex security deposits within limits the CFTC provides [@cftc2010].

terms.simple: A warning from your broker that you have lost so much that your deposit is too small, so you must add money or close trades.
terms.analogy: Like the bike shop calling to say the deposit no longer covers the damage.
terms.precise: A demand to restore margin above the maintenance level. Retail FX and CFD brokers often skip the call and close positions automatically at a stop-out level.

terms.simple: When the broker closes your trades for you because your account fell too low.
terms.analogy: Like a referee stopping a boxing match before someone gets badly hurt.
terms.precise: Automatic liquidation at a set margin level. ESMA's retail CFD rules require brokers to close positions once account equity falls to 50% of the required margin [@url-46fb23ac]. The fill can still be far from that level in a fast market.

terms.simple: A rule that you cannot lose more than the money in your account.
terms.analogy: Like a safety net under a trampoline: you can fall, but not below the net.
terms.precise: A requirement that retail clients' losses are capped at the funds in their account, part of ESMA's 2018 CFD measures [@url-46fb23ac]. It does not exist everywhere; after the Swiss franc floor was removed in January 2015, some clients ended with negative balances [@snb2015].

terms.simple: An order that closes your trade automatically if the price moves against you by a set amount.
terms.analogy: Like a smoke alarm that goes off before the whole house burns.
terms.precise: An order to exit once a price is reached. It becomes a market order, so in a gap it fills at the next available price, which may be much worse. FX stop orders cluster just beyond round numbers [@osler2003].

terms.simple: An order that closes your trade automatically once it has made a set amount.
terms.analogy: Like deciding before a game that you will leave the arcade once you win ten tickets.
terms.precise: A limit order to exit at a target price. In FX these cluster at round numbers, which may be one reason trends often pause there [@osler2003].

terms.simple: A stop loss that moves up as the price moves in your favour, but never moves back down.
terms.analogy: Like a climber's rope clipped higher as they climb, so a fall is never all the way to the bottom.
terms.precise: A stop set a fixed distance or volatility multiple behind the best price since entry. It turns any trade into a simple trend rule on exit.

terms.simple: The difference between the price you expected and the price you actually got.
terms.analogy: Like ordering a 2 pound sandwich and being charged 2.10 because the price changed while you queued.
terms.precise: Execution price minus the reference price at the time of the decision. It rises with order size, volatility and thin markets, and is part of total transaction costs.

terms.simple: The danger that the price jumps past your stop loss, so you lose more than you planned.
terms.analogy: Like planning to step off a moving walkway at a certain spot, but the floor drops away first.
terms.precise: Loss from discontinuous price moves. On 15 January 2015 the Swiss National Bank removed its 1.20 franc per euro floor [@snb2015], and the franc moved so far so fast that many stops filled far from their levels.

terms.simple: A measure of how much the price usually moves in one period.
terms.analogy: Like knowing a river usually rises and falls about half a metre a day.
terms.precise: The average over N periods of the true range: the largest of high minus low, high minus previous close, and previous close minus low. Used to set stops and position sizes in units of typical movement.

terms.simple: Making trades smaller when the price is jumpy and bigger when it is calm, so each trade carries about the same risk.
terms.analogy: Like walking more carefully on ice and striding out on dry pavement.
terms.precise: Size each position inversely to its forecast volatility. Moreira and Muir (2017) found scaling exposure by inverse variance raised Sharpe ratios for several factors [@moreira2017]. It is the core of Carver's sizing method [@carver2015].

terms.simple: How much you could win on a trade compared with how much you could lose.
terms.analogy: Like a bet where you risk 1 sweet to win 3.
terms.precise: Distance to target divided by distance to stop. A high ratio is not good by itself: with a low enough chance of reaching the target the expected value is still negative. Only ratio and win rate together give expectancy.

terms.simple: The average amount you expect to win or lose per trade over many trades.
terms.analogy: Like working out that a game where you win 1 pound half the time and lose 2 pounds the other half costs you 50p a go.
terms.precise: Win rate times average win minus loss rate times average loss, after costs. A strategy can win most trades and still have negative expectancy, or win few and be positive.

terms.simple: The risk of very rare but very big moves.
terms.analogy: Like the chance of a hundred-year flood: rare, but it can wipe out everything at once.
terms.precise: Risk from extreme outcomes far from the average. Mandelbrot (1963) proposed replacing the normal distribution of price changes with fatter-tailed stable laws [@mandelbrot1963]. Carry trades are a known example of strategies with crash risk [@brunnermeier2008].

terms.simple: Doubling your bet after every loss so that one win gets everything back.
terms.analogy: Like chasing a runaway ball downhill faster and faster: it works until you trip.
terms.precise: A system that doubles stake after each loss. It turns many small wins into rare total losses, because capital or limits run out before the streak ends [@feller1968]. It does not change the expected value of the game.

terms.simple: Buying more of something after its price falls, to lower your average price.
terms.analogy: Like ordering more of a meal you did not like because the second plate is cheaper.
terms.precise: Adding to a losing position. It lowers the average entry price but raises exposure to a trade that is going wrong. Without a rule set in advance, it is a form of escalation of commitment [@staw1976].

terms.simple: Adding to a trade that is already making money.
terms.analogy: Like adding more bricks to a wall only after the first layer has set.
terms.precise: Increasing a winning position in steps. It is the opposite of averaging down and is common in trend following. It still raises total exposure, so total risk must be capped.

terms.simple: The danger that trades you thought were separate all go wrong together.
terms.analogy: Like carrying eggs in five baskets that are all tied to the same rope.
terms.precise: Risk that positions move together more than expected, especially in stress. Most FX trades share the US dollar on one side (89.2% in April 2025 [@bis2025]), and a common dollar factor explains much of the movement of currencies [@lustig2011].

terms.simple: Checking what would happen to your money in a really bad scenario.
terms.analogy: Like a fire drill: practise the disaster before it happens.
terms.precise: Revaluing a portfolio under extreme but plausible moves, either historical (for example January 2015 in the franc, 2008 in carry trades) or made up. It complements VaR, which says little about extremes [@jorion2006].

terms.simple: Earning returns on your earlier returns, so money grows faster and faster over time.
terms.analogy: Like a snowball rolling downhill, picking up more snow the bigger it gets.
terms.precise: Growth where each period's return applies to the accumulated value: final value equals start times the product of (1 plus r) over all periods. It works the same way on losses, which is why big losses are so costly.

terms.simple: The plain average of returns: add them up and divide by how many there are.
terms.analogy: Like averaging your test scores. It can look better than how much you actually learned over the year.
terms.precise: The simple average of period returns. It overstates what an investor actually earns over time when returns vary: +50% then -50% averages 0% but leaves you 25% down.

terms.simple: The steady yearly growth rate that would turn your starting money into your ending money.
terms.analogy: Like working out the one constant speed that would get you to the finish in the same time as your stop-start drive.
terms.precise: The nth root of the product of (1 plus r) minus 1. It is always at or below the arithmetic mean, and roughly equal to the arithmetic mean minus half the variance [@messmore1995]. Over years it is the same as CAGR.

terms.simple: Big ups and downs make your money grow slower than the average return suggests.
terms.analogy: Like a car that speeds up and brakes a lot: it uses more fuel and gets there later than one that drives steadily.
terms.precise: The gap between arithmetic and geometric mean returns, about half the variance per period (also called variance drain) [@messmore1995]. A strategy with 10% average return and 30% volatility compounds at roughly 10% minus 4.5%, or 5.5%, a year.

terms.simple: How much your money grew in plain numbers, without thinking about prices going up.
terms.analogy: Like getting a bigger allowance without noticing sweets got more expensive too.
terms.precise: Return measured in currency units, before adjusting for inflation.

terms.simple: How much more stuff your money can buy after accounting for rising prices.
terms.analogy: Like checking how many more sweets your bigger allowance actually buys.
terms.precise: Nominal return adjusted for inflation: (1 plus nominal) divided by (1 plus inflation) minus 1, roughly nominal minus inflation. Long-run studies of world markets report real returns because nominal figures mislead across eras [@dimson2002].

terms.simple: When prices of things in shops go up over time, so the same money buys less.
terms.analogy: Like a bag of crisps that costs a bit more every year.
terms.precise: The rate of change of a price index such as the consumer price index. Differences in inflation between countries are the base of purchasing power parity.

terms.simple: A return turned into a 'per year' number so that different time periods can be compared.
terms.analogy: Like saying a runner's pace in kilometres per hour even if they only ran for ten minutes.
terms.precise: For compounding: (1 plus total return) to the power (1 divided by years) minus 1. Annualising a short, lucky period gives huge and misleading numbers.

terms.simple: How jumpy returns are, scaled to a one-year number.
terms.analogy: Like converting a daily wobble into a yearly wobble so you can compare a boat and a ship.
terms.precise: Standard deviation of period returns times the square root of periods per year (about 252 trading days or 52 weeks), assuming returns are independent. Volatility grows with the square root of time, not with time.

terms.simple: A way of measuring returns that lets you just add them up over time.
terms.analogy: Like measuring a journey in steps you can add, instead of percentages of the distance left.
terms.precise: The natural log of (end price divided by start price). Log returns add across time, and a +x and -x log return cancel exactly, unlike simple returns.

terms.simple: How much the price changed as a percent: end minus start, divided by start.
terms.analogy: Like saying your height went from 100 cm to 110 cm, a 10% gain.
terms.precise: (P1 minus P0) divided by P0. Simple returns add across assets in a portfolio but not across time; log returns add across time but not across assets.

terms.simple: After you lose some money, you need a bigger percent gain to get back to where you started.
terms.analogy: Like a ball dropped from a height: losing half needs doubling to get back up.
terms.precise: To recover from a loss L you need a gain of L divided by (1 minus L): 10% needs 11.1%, 25% needs 33.3%, 50% needs 100% and 90% needs 900%.

terms.simple: A shortcut: divide 72 by the yearly percent return to guess how many years it takes to double your money.
terms.analogy: At 8% a year, 72 divided by 8 is 9, so about 9 years to double.
terms.precise: An approximation to ln(2) divided by ln(1 plus r), accurate for rates around 6% to 10%. It also gives how fast inflation halves purchasing power.

terms.simple: The return you could get with almost no risk, like a short loan to the government.
terms.analogy: Like the interest from keeping money in the safest piggy bank there is.
terms.precise: Usually the yield on short-dated government bills in the relevant currency. Excess returns and the Sharpe ratio are measured over it. A strategy that does not beat it has earned nothing for the risk taken.

terms.simple: What you give up by choosing one thing instead of another.
terms.analogy: If you spend Saturday at the cinema, you cannot also spend it at the beach.
terms.precise: The value of the best foregone alternative. For a trading strategy, the alternatives are cash at the risk-free rate and a cheap index fund; our S&P 500 benchmark is the second.

terms.simple: A fee charged every year as a percent of the money a fund manages, whether it makes money or not.
terms.analogy: Like paying a gardener a fixed amount each month, even in months nothing grows.
terms.precise: An annual charge on assets under management. French (2008) estimated US investors spent about 0.67% of the total market value each year trying to beat the market, and that a typical investor would have done better in a passive fund [@french2008].

terms.simple: A fee taken as a share of the profits a fund makes.
terms.analogy: Like a coach who takes a cut of your prize money.
terms.precise: A share of returns above a hurdle, often 20%, usually charged only above a high-water mark. It is asymmetric: the manager shares gains but not losses, which can encourage risk taking.

terms.simple: The highest value an account or fund has reached. Performance fees are usually only paid on gains above it.
terms.analogy: Like the line a flood leaves on a wall: the water has to rise above it to count as a new record.
terms.precise: The peak net asset value used to compute performance fees and drawdowns. A fund below its high-water mark is in drawdown.

terms.simple: Gross return is before costs and fees. Net return is what you actually keep.
terms.analogy: Like the price on a payslip before tax, and what lands in your bank.
terms.precise: Gross minus trading costs, fees, financing and taxes equals net. Barber and Odean (2000) found frequent traders' gross returns were close to the market but net returns far below it [@barber2000].
